idiom_name: Node base class + one subclass per grammar rule implementing interpret(context)
implementation_notes: Ruby's dynamic dispatch makes the GoF shape cheap to write: a Node base class declaring interpret(context), one subclass per rule, and a parser that builds the tree (the SIF paper's Node.build does exactly this). Blocks and lambdas are the lightweight substitute for terminal nodes, since any object answering call can act as a procedure; keep the class form when each rule needs its own validation or state.
pitfalls: Open classes let any code add or replace interpret on a core type; convenient for extending a language, lethal for predictability - restrict monkey patches to your own namespace.
Deep recursion raises SystemStackError and Ruby gives no tail-call optimisation by default, which the SIF paper notes as a real shortcoming for recursive interpreters.
method_missing and define_method tricks hide the grammar from any static reading; keep the node set explicit if tooling must see it.

variants.name: Plain data nodes evaluated by case/in pattern matching
variants.idiom_name: arrays/hashes or Structs plus one recursive case/in evaluator
variants.implementation_notes: Ruby 3.0 added case/in pattern matching with array, hash and find patterns and the deconstruct protocol, so nodes can be plain tuples or Structs and evaluation a single recursive case/in. This is the form to pick when the AST is data and several passes (evaluate, print, collect variables) will walk it, or when trees arrive deserialised from JSON; the class-per-node form stays better when each rule carries validation and behaviour.
variants.code_sketch:
def eval_node(node, ctx)
  case node
  in [:num, value] then value
  in [:add, left, right] then eval_node(left, ctx) + eval_node(right, ctx)
  in [:var, name] then ctx.fetch(name)
  else raise ArgumentError, "unhandled node: #{node.inspect}"
  end
end
pitfalls: Array patterns match on structure alone, so a node with the wrong arity falls through to else; every case/in evaluator needs an else that raises.
Hash patterns ignore extra keys unless a find pattern (**) is used, so a misspelled node key can pass unnoticed and evaluate to nil.
Distinguishing node kinds by positional structure makes the grammar's shape implicit; prefer a leading tag symbol in every node for readable patterns.
